aprendizado-de-maquina.d: Fitting the parameters \( \theta \) of a function \( f_\theta \) to examples, by minimizing a loss function, so that it also does well on data it has never seen.

hiperparametro.d: A choice made by humans before training, which the gradient does not adjust: the shape of the model, the learning rate, the batch size, the weights of each term in the loss. Distinct from the parameters (weights), which training learns.

aprendizado-supervisionado.d: Training on (input, desired answer) pairs in which the answer was supplied from outside, usually by human annotators. It is expensive to scale. The SFT stage of an LLM's post-training is supervised.

aprendizado-auto-supervisionado.d: Training in which the data itself supplies the label. In an LLM: hide the next token and ask the model to predict it. A text of \( N \) tokens yields \( N-1 \) examples with no human annotation.

pre-treino.d: The giant self-supervised phase in which the model learns to predict the next token over trillions of tokens of text. DeepSeek-V4 used more than 32T. It produces a “text completer”.

pos-treino.d: The phases that turn the pre-trained model into an assistant: SFT (instruction → response pairs), reinforcement learning (e.g. GRPO) and distillation. They use the same mechanics of loss, gradient and optimizer.

funcao-de-perda.d: A number that measures how wrong the model is on average over the examples, \( \mathcal{L}(\theta) \). Training is the search for the parameters that minimize it. In LLMs, it is the next-token cross-entropy.

mse.d: \( \tfrac1N\sum_i (f_\theta(x_i)-y_i)^2 \): the mean of the squared residuals. It is the standard loss for predicting continuous numbers: it punishes large errors disproportionately and is smooth.

logits.d: Raw scores the model gives each option before the softmax. In an LLM there is one per vocabulary token, produced by the lm_head from the final hidden state (\( z = W_U h \)). They can be negative, and only the differences between them matter. The softmax turns them into probabilities.

softmax.d: A function that turns real scores into positive weights that add up to 1: \( p_j = e^{z_j}/\sum_k e^{z_k} \). The highest score takes the largest share, but none gets zero. It does not change if the same constant is added to every score, which is what lets you compute it without overflow by subtracting the maximum. It shows up at the model's output, in attention and in sampling.

entropia-cruzada.d: \( H(P,Q) = -\sum_v P(v)\ln Q(v) \): the average surprise of using distribution \( Q \) to predict what \( P \) generates. With \( P \) concentrated on the right token \( y \), it becomes \( -\ln Q(y) \), the training loss of an LLM. It equals \( H(P) + D_{KL}(P\|Q) \): whatever exceeds the entropy of \( P \) is the KLD, the distance between the two distributions, which the recipes use to measure quantizations.

nll.d: The mean of \( -\ln p_\theta(x_t\mid x_{<t}) \) over the positions of a text: the average surprise at the true tokens. It is the very cross-entropy loss used in training; minimizing it means maximizing the likelihood of the data.

nats.d: Unit of information measured with the natural logarithm: 1 nat = 1/ln 2 ≈ 1.443 bit. Training losses (PyTorch uses ln) and the recipes' KLDs and NLLs are reported in nats per position (or per token).

perplexidade.d: \( e^{\text{NLL}} \): the effective number of options the model seems to hesitate between (an NLL of 1.59 nat ≈ 4.9 options). It is only comparable on the same text with the same tokenizer, and it hides errors that cancel out in the average.

superficie-de-perda.d: The loss seen as a function of the parameters, with the data fixed: a “relief map” in which each point is a configuration of weights. Training is descending into a valley of that relief.

gradiente.d: The vector of partial derivatives of the loss with respect to each parameter, \( \nabla_\theta\mathcal{L} \). It points to where the loss rises fastest. In networks, it is computed by backpropagation.

descida-do-gradiente.d: The update \( \theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\nabla_\theta\mathcal{L} \): a small step against the gradient, repeated until the loss stops falling. It is the basis of every deep learning optimizer.

taxa-de-aprendizado.d: The step size of gradient descent. Too small, and training is slow; too large, and it oscillates or diverges (in a quadratic valley, it requires \( \eta < 2/\lambda_{\max} \)). It usually follows a schedule: warmup, plateau and decay.

minibatch.d: A small sample of examples used to estimate the gradient in one training step. In LLMs it is measured in tokens. Not to be confused with the batch of requests of an inference server.

sgd.d: Gradient descent using the mean gradient of a randomly sampled minibatch instead of the exact gradient. The estimate is unbiased, and its noise falls as \( 1/\sqrt{B} \).

epoca.d: One full pass over all the training data. In LLM pre-training it is common to see each token only once, or a few times.

otimizador.d: The rule that turns gradients into weight updates (SGD, momentum, Adam/AdamW, Muon). Its state, such as Adam's moments, exists only during training and does not go into the checkpoint.

momentum.d: Accumulating a “velocity” \( v \leftarrow \beta v + g \) that is used instead of the raw gradient. It cancels oscillations between the walls of a valley and accelerates along its floor. Typically \( \beta \approx 0.9 \).

adam.d: An optimizer that keeps moving averages of the gradient (\( m \)) and of its square (\( s \)) per coordinate and takes steps \( \eta\,\hat m/(\sqrt{\hat s}+\epsilon) \): each parameter moves on the order of \( \eta \) per step, whatever the scale of its gradient.

adamw.d: Adam with decoupled weight decay: the \( \lambda\theta \) term is applied outside the division by \( \sqrt{\hat s} \). It was the standard for training Transformers. In Qwen3.8 and DeepSeek-V4 it handles embeddings, heads and norms, while Muon handles the matrices.

weight-decay.d: Pulling every weight a little toward zero at each step (\( -\eta\lambda\theta \)), which is equivalent to penalizing \( \tfrac\lambda2\lVert\theta\rVert^2 \). It is a form of regularization that reduces overfitting.

muon.d: An optimizer for matrix-shaped parameters: it accumulates the momentum \( M \) and applies the nearest orthogonal matrix, \( \approx UV^\top \), computed by Newton–Schulz. Every singular direction gets the same step. Used to train Qwen3.8 and DeepSeek-V4.

valores-singulares.d: In the decomposition \( M = U\Sigma V^\top \), the numbers on the diagonal of \( \Sigma \): how much the matrix stretches each of its principal directions. \( U \) and \( V \) are rotations; an orthogonal matrix has all its singular values equal to 1.

newton-schulz.d: Approximate orthogonalization using only matrix multiplications: \( X \leftarrow aX + b(XX^\top)X + c(XX^\top)^2X \), which applies \( a\sigma+b\sigma^3+c\sigma^5 \) to each singular value. Muon uses (3.4445, −4.7750, 2.0315); DeepSeek-V4 runs 8 of these iterations and 2 polishing ones with (2, −1.5, 0.5).

loss-spike.d: A sudden jump in the loss during training, sometimes unrecoverable, often linked to exploding attention logits or to a learning rate that is too high. The Qwen3.8 report counts spikes per 10,000 steps to compare training recipes.

qk-clip.d: A training trick used with Muon (described in the Kimi K2 technical report, a source outside the recipe inventories): when the largest attention logit crosses a threshold, \( W_Q \) and \( W_K \) are scaled down. Qwen3.8 does without the trick thanks to QK-Norm; DeepSeek-V4, thanks to a weightless RMSNorm on each head of \( q \) and a kv_norm on the KV latent.

generalizacao.d: The ability to get right answers on data the model did not see in training. It is measured on a separate set (validation/test). It is the real goal of learning; the training loss is just a means.

treino-validacao-teste.d: Splitting the data into three parts: training (fits the weights), validation (picks hyperparameters and when to stop) and test (stays locked away until the end and gives the honest grade). If the test set leaks into training, the grade measures memory.

underfitting.d: A model too rigid for the pattern in the data: it makes large errors on both training and validation. Remedy: more capacity (more parameters) or more training.

overfitting.d: A model that memorizes the noise in the training examples: the training loss falls, but the validation loss rises. Remedies: more data, regularization (weight decay) and early stopping.

regularizacao.d: Any technique that discourages overly complicated solutions in order to improve generalization: a \( \lambda\lVert\theta\rVert^2 \) penalty (weight decay), early stopping, more data.

bce.d: A loss for a predicted probability \( c \) (the output of a sigmoid) against a target \( c^* \in [0,1] \): \( -[c^*\ln c + (1-c^*)\ln(1-c)] \). It trained DSpark's confidence head against \( c^* = 1-\mathrm{TV}(p,q) \).

ste.d: A QAT trick: in the backward, it treats rounding (a staircase, with zero derivative almost everywhere) as if it were the identity, \( \partial\hat w/\partial w \approx 1 \), so that the gradient can get through.

inferencia.d: Using the trained model: only the forward, with no loss, no gradient and no optimizer. It is all the recipes do. They choose how to compute the forward, not what it computes.

forward-pass.d: Computing the model's output from the input, layer by layer, with the current weights. In training it is followed by the backward. At inference it is the only thing that runs.

pesos-congelados.d: Weights that no longer change: the state of a served checkpoint. Edits like abliteration are algebra on frozen weights, not training.
